To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the villin subdomain folds via a three-state mechanism with the transition states of the fast and slow phases located at the same point along the reaction coordinate and that the folding rate constant is determined by the diffusion rate along the reaction coordinate.

the villin subdomain folds via a two-state mechanism, the folding free energy barrier is ∼6 kcal/mol, the transition state has ∼50% of the native contacts and ∼50% native secondary structure, the folding time is ∼1 μs, the folding time for a residue is ∼1 ns, and the free-energy surface is highly cooperative, with a large number of residues changing simultaneously.

the folding of this protein is a two-stage process with a barrier of 6.4 kcal/mol, that the transition-state ensemble consists of 10-15% folded structure, and that the folding process is a diffusion on a free-energy surface with a barrier of only 1.4 kcal/mol and an energy difference of only 0.7 kcal/mol between the folded and unfolded minima.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the folding mechanism and the free-energy landscape of a protein.

the elucidation of the mechanism of protein folding and unfolding by combining the experimental and theoretical tools of chemical and physical kinetics with the theoretical tools of statistical mechanics and computer simulation.

the elucidation of the structure and dynamics of proteins, and the methods used are equilibrium and nonequilibrium spectroscopy, molecular-dynamics simulations, and chemical, physical, and statistical-thermodynamic models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Ising-like theoretical kinetics model is the most accurate model for the folding of the villin subdomain, and it is the only model that is able to explain all of the experimental observations.
the villin subdomain is an ultrafast folding two-state protein, but that the transition state is not well defined and the free-energy barrier is low.
the three-state chemical- kinetics model is the simplest, the theoretical model is the most complete, and the physical-kinetic model lies between these two extremes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
all three types of models provide a consistent picture of the folding mechanism of the villin subdomain.
the three models provide complementary views of the folding mechanism.

the data for this system are consistent with a model in which folding proceeds by a diffusion on a one-dimension surface, with the order parameters for the reaction coordinate being the fraction of native residues, and the free-energy barrier is ∼10 kcal/mol.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a combination of experimental data, theoretical models, and physical intuition is needed to understand protein folding and design.
the theoretical model provides the most detailed and most accurate description of the folding process.

the physical-kinetic and theoretical models provide a more complete and detailed description of protein folding than the chemical-kinetic model, and the latter is not needed for an understanding of the mechanism of folding of villin subdomain.
